newsitem.title: USA: Shell, Texaco confirm talks on linkup.
newsitem.headline: Shell, Texaco confirm talks on linkup.

text.p: Texaco Inc. and Shell Oil Co. said Monday they were in talks about linking their refining and marketing operations in the United States, a deal that could be the first of several big mergers in the domestic refining industry.

The two oil giants said the talks included Star Enterprise, Texaco's joint venture with the state-owned Saudi Aramco, which would virtually guarantee future supplies from Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest oil producer.
Texaco said the goal of the talks was to create a more efficient, competitive operation building on the strengths of both companies, including their well-known brand names.
But industry analysts said tough competition in the refining business, where too much capacity and rising crude oil prices have driven down profits, was clearly driving the negotiations.
"In the U.S., refining margins have been absolutely miserable in the last couple of months," said Paul Ting at Salomon Brothers.
"If oil prices continue to move higher it is going to maintain the pressure ... and refiners are going to be the ones biggest hit," said Steve Pfeiffer, an analyst at Paine Webber.

Big oil companies' stock prices have soared as crude oil prices have risen. But gasoline prices have failed to keep pace, which means that companies that refine oil have earned less as they have had to pay more for crude.

A merger of all or part of the three companies' refining and marketing operations would save at least $1 billion a year and create the biggest marketer in the world's biggest oil- and gas-consuming nation.

It would also be the largest merger in the refining and marketing business to date in the United States. Earlier his year Mobil Corp. and British Petroleum Plc agreed to merge their refining and marketing operations in Europe.
The latest talks were first reported in Monday's Wall Street Journal, which cited people close to the negotiations.

A merger of all three companies' refining operations would combine about $17 billion of assets and bring together Shell's 8,700 outlets with Texaco/Star's 14,000 service stations in the United States, analysts said. In addition, Shell runs five refineries while Star and Texaco operate seven plants.
The operation would have about 15 percent of the domestic market for gasoline and refined products overall, the analysts said.

"A merger would be positive in two ways," said Paine Webber's Pfeiffer. "It would result in a cost saving of $1 billion-plus. And they would reap the benefits of having the largest market presence in the country."
If a merger were announced, the Federal Trade Commission or the Justice Department would be certain to review the proposal for antitrust implications, an FTC spokesman said Monday.
The companies gave no indication of when a deal might be announced, but the Journal said in its report that it could be months before an agreement was signed.
Investors cheered the news and drove Texaco stock up $1 to $96.625 on the New York Stock Exchange. Shares of Shell Transport and Trading in London also rose.
Other similar mergers could follow, analysts said.

While talks between Phillips Petroleum Co. and Conoco Inc. about combining marketing and refining stalled in June, Atlantic Richfield Co. and Unocal Corp. have said they want to expand from their base on the West Coast.
In addition, last month two smaller refiners, Ultramar Corp. and Diamond Shamrock Inc., announced a merger that would create a company with a market value of about $2.3 billion.

"In the last three or four years there has been only about 600,000 barrels a day of capacity taken out (of the U.S. industry)," said Salomon Brothers' Ting. "This could be a very interesting litmus test of what the industry is going to do."

"Shell Oil Co. confirms it is discussing with Texaco the potential for joint arrangements involving U.S. downstream operations," Shell said in its statement. "While the companies are reviewing a range of options concerning the businesses that might be included, no decisions have been made."
Texaco also confirmed discussions about a possible alliance. Officials of the two companies declined to elaborate.
CS First Boston Corp. was advising Texaco, Morgan Stanley & Co. was Shell's investment bank and J.P. Morgan & Co. was advising Star, the Journal said.
